say: Welcome back, detectives! Today the clues are the signs: +, −, × and ÷, and the brackets that boss them around.
The same numbers can give very different answers. Our job is to find out why, and to make numbers do what we want. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
Here are four cards: 2, 4, 5 and 9. You can use each card once, with plus, minus, times or divide.
When a target appears, race to hit it on your whiteboard. Then look for a second way!
Look at 6 + 4 × 3 − 2. If you can put ONE pair of brackets anywhere, how many different answers do you think you can make? Write your guess in the corner of your whiteboard.
stuck: Stuck: put the brackets round 6 + 4 first. What do you work out first now?
Not sure if you have them all: "Make a list of every place the brackets can go: round two numbers, round three numbers."
Finished early: can TWO pairs of brackets make a new answer?

say: "40 − 8 × 3 + 6 ÷ 2. No brackets, so I look for × and ÷ first: 8 × 3 is 24 and 6 ÷ 2 is 3. Now I have 40 − 24 + 3. Only + and − are left, so I go from left to right: 16, then 19."
"8, 5 and 3 must make 37. Even adding all three only makes 16, so there must be a times. 8 × 5 is 40, and 40 − 3 is 37. Let me check by doing it in the right order: 8 × 5 − 3 = 37."
"21 came out of the machine. The last step was divide by 2, so I undo it: times 2 gives 42. Then undo take away 6: add 6, 48. Then undo times 4: divide by 4, 12. I check by going forwards."

do: Ask: "Which part do you work out first? Point to it and underline it."
Ask: "Is your target big or small compared with the numbers? What does that tell you?"
Ask: "What is the opposite of this step? How do you undo it?"
stuck: Hint 1: "Underline the part in brackets, then the × and ÷ parts. Do those first."
Hint 2: "Estimate first. A big target usually needs a ×. Try one sign, then test it."
Hint 3: "Working backwards, start at the END and undo each step: × becomes ÷, − becomes +."

say: "Ben says 20 − 8 + 2 = 10 because you add first. Mei says 14. Who is right?"
ask: "Ben says 20 − 8 + 2 = 10 because you add first. Mei says 14. Who is right?"
Mei is right. When there are only + and − (or only × and ÷), we work from left to right: 20 − 8 = 12, then 12 + 2 = 14. Ben worked out 8 + 2 first, which would need brackets: 20 − (8 + 2) = 10.

say: "Today you made the signs and brackets work for you, and you worked backwards like real detectives."
"Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal."

p4l3-title.note: Objective: Use the order of operations (brackets first, then × and ÷ from left to right, then + and − from left to right), find missing signs and brackets to hit a target, work backwards through a chain of operations, and solve "times as many" problems with a bar model. Thinking strategies taught today: ESTIMATE, TEST AND ADJUST (guess and check), WORK BACKWARDS and DRAW A BAR MODEL. Materials: mini whiteboards and markers; paper number cards 0 to 9; sign cards +, −, ×, ÷ and two pairs of bracket cards per child; scrap paper for bar models. Online: children write on whiteboards and say the answer together on three; before the lesson they cut out the sign and bracket cards so they can move them on camera in the explore task. Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 3-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 23.5 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 23.5 to 28.5 (click to reveal each step and answer; there is no "your turn" slide today). Brain break 28.5 to 32.5 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 32.5 to 80.5: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 32.5 to 49, check together 49 to 51, short teaching before page 2 51 to 53.5, page 2 on your own 53.5 to 76.5 (the last 3 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 76.5 to 80.5. Talk time 80.5 to 85 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 85 to 87.5. Looking back 87.5 to 90 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). Pairs: Q1 and Q2. Then Q3 alone. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today's tool is Guess and check. Make a sensible guess, check it against every clue, improve it. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p4l3-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) 11 sweets: 2 × 4 + 3 = 8 + 3 = 11. The bags are counted first (×), then the loose sweets are added (+). 2) (2 + 3) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20. With no brackets the answer is 14, because 3 × 4 is done first. A GOOD REASON: A story helps: the bags are counted first, then the loose ones are added. Brackets change which part is done first. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "Pairs: Q1 and Q2. Then Q3 alone. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l3-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Target Numbers. Children copy the four cards 2, 4, 5 and 9 onto their whiteboards. Point to one target at a time: "Make 13. Go!" Everyone writes a sentence and reads it aloud together on three: there is no race and no points. Click to show one way for each target (clicks reveal 13, 22, 36, 81 in order). Other ways: 13 = 2 × 9 − 5; 22 = 2 × 9 + 4; 81 needs brackets: (4 + 5) × 9. Listen for children who write 2 + 4 × 5 and say 30: they added first. That leads straight into today's lesson. Finisher: "Can you make 100?" (Let them try; it cannot be done with these cards and signs, which is a good thing to notice.)

p4l3-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Mental maths, three questions, about 30 seconds each. Read each aloud, write it, say the answer together on three, then click. No follow-up questions. Answers: 100, 8, 54. The other two warm-up questions (1 000 − 368; 4 × 20) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l3-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 20.5. Pairs work with number, sign and bracket cards (online: paper cards on camera, or write on whiteboards). Ask them to predict first: how many different answers? Many children guess 5 or 6, one for each place. Let them try any placement; the brackets must go round at least two numbers. Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: can TWO pairs of brackets make a new answer? ((6 + 4) × (3 − 2) = 10, the same as one of the others.) GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): What if you may use TWO pairs of brackets? Can you get an answer that one pair could not? Answer: No. Two pairs still give only 16, 28 and 10 (every placement checked by computer). Brackets only change what is done first, and here there are only three different orders that matter: the × first (16), (6 + 4) first (28) or (3 − 2) first (10).

p4l3-explore2.note: Minutes 20.5 to 23.5. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather the answers on the board. Two debrief questions only. Answers: 1) Only 3 different answers: 16 (no brackets), 28 and 10. 2) Biggest: (6 + 4) × 3 − 2 = 10 × 3 − 2 = 28. Smallest: 6 + 4 × (3 − 2) = 6 + 4 × 1 = 10. The third question (which brackets do not change the answer? Brackets round 4 × 3, round 6 + 4 × 3, or round 4 × 3 − 2 all give 16, because the × is done first anyway) is answered by the first teaching slide, so it is not asked here. Do NOT teach the rule yet if nobody says it: the next slides teach it.

p4l3-teach1.note: Teach. Read the order together. Children work out the example on whiteboards first, then click through the steps. Think-aloud: "No brackets, so I look for × and ÷ first: 8 × 3 is 24 and 6 ÷ 2 is 3. Now I only have + and −, so I go from left to right: 40 − 24 is 16, and 16 + 3 is 19." The last click shows the common mistake: doing everything from left to right. Ask: "Which part did this child do first? Why is that wrong?"

p4l3-we1.note: Strategy: ESTIMATE, TEST, ADJUST. Ask first: "Is 37 big or small compared with 8, 5 and 3? What does that tell us?" Click through: step 1, step 2, the signs appear in the circles, step 3, the answer. Think-aloud: "If I add everything I only get 16, so I need a times. 8 × 5 is 40, that is just 3 too many, so take away 3." Remind them to CHECK in the right order: 8 × 5 − 3 means 40 − 3, not 8 × 2.

p4l3-we2.note: Strategy: test and adjust. Think-aloud: "19 is too small. Brackets let me add BEFORE I multiply, which makes the multiplication bigger. Round 2 + 3 gives 25. Round 4 + 5 gives 29. Found it." (Two pairs of brackets would give (2 + 3) × (4 + 5) = 45; with one pair, 29.)

p4l3-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Working strictly from left to right and ignoring the order: 40 − 8 × 3 done as 32 × 3. (2) Thinking addition always comes before subtraction (or × before ÷) instead of working left to right: 20 − 8 + 2 answered 10, 72 ÷ 8 × 3 answered 3. (3) Working backwards but using the same operation instead of the opposite one (for − 18, taking away 18 again instead of adding 18).

p4l3-break.note: 4 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 32.5): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Read each sentence, count down from 3, everyone moves. Answers: 3 + 4 × 2 = 11 (odd, crouch); (3 + 4) × 2 = 14 (even, stand); 20 ÷ 4 + 1 = 6 (even, stand); 20 ÷ (4 + 1) = 4 (even, stand). Online: children stand up and crouch on camera.

p4l3-ws1.note: Minutes 32.5 to 49. Pairs do Q1 and Q2 (about 9 minutes of work). Q3 is the first question each child does on their own, at the start of page 2 time; its answer is checked together with page 2. Walk around. Ask "Which part do you work out first?" before giving any help. Q2d has four numbers: encourage children to test a sign in the first circle and see how big the answer is so far. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "Pairs: Q1 and Q2. Then Q3 alone. After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l3-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q1d: 45 ÷ 5 = 9 first, then 100 − 9 + 7 = 98 (not 55 ÷ 5 + 7). Q1e: 6 × 8 ÷ 4 = 48 ÷ 4 = 12. Q2d: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and 2 × 5 = 10, 4 + 10 = 14; each puzzle on this page has only one answer.

p4l3-teachback.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4). Only two methods are taught before page 2 (this one and the bar model). The chain slide for Q7, a choice question, is in the take-home pack. Strategy: WORK BACKWARDS. Start at the END. Each step is undone with the opposite operation: × and ÷ undo each other, + and − undo each other. Ask before each click: "What was the last thing the machine did? How do we undo it?" Watch for children who take away 6 again instead of adding 6. Always check by going forwards.

p4l3-teachbar.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q6). Strategy: DRAW A BAR MODEL. Draw Ben's bar first (1 unit), then Ali's bar with 4 units the same size. The brace shows the total. Ask: "How many units altogether? What is one unit worth?" Show the division on the board: 1 345 ÷ 5 = 269 (13 hundreds ÷ 5 = 2 hundreds r 3 hundreds; 34 tens ÷ 5 = 6 tens r 4 tens; 45 ÷ 5 = 9). Extra question: "How many MORE stickers does Ali have?" (3 units = 807).

p4l3-teachchain.note: Take-home pack (Q7 is a choice question that is not taught in the lesson; any child who picks it can use this slide). Read the example aloud. Left: when two numbers next to each other are known, work backwards by taking away. Right: when the gaps are in the middle, guess the 2nd number and test it, then adjust: 12 was too small and 18 too big, so the answer is in between. Ask: "When I add 1 to my guess, how much does the 4th number go up?" (by 2, because the guess is used twice). That helps strong children find it in one step.

p4l3-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson, especially children who undo − with − when working backwards. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Do question 3 first, then Q4, Q5 and Q6. Q7 (★) is a choice, for take-home. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 3 minutes of this block (minute 73.5 to 76.5) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l3-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3 (brackets, done first on their own): a) 4 + 8 × 5 − 3 = 41; b) (4 + 8) × 5 − 3 = 57; c) 4 + 8 × (5 − 3) = 20. Q4 check: 23 × 6 = 138, − 18 = 120, ÷ 4 = 30. Q5: with 3: 15, 50, 10, 7. Part b is now a fill-in: number, 7, 7 (the open "explain why" is the Think harder stretch). Bar model: five bars of your number plus 35; shared into 5 groups, each group is one bar and 7; take away the bar and 7 is left. Q6: chicken rice 3 units, laksa 1 unit; 124 ÷ 4 = 31; 3 × 31 = 93; the difference is 2 units = 62. (The old 1 236 version, 309 / 927 / 618, is in the question bank.) Q7b: try 7 for the 2nd number: 4, 7, 11, 18.

p4l3-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) 468 (5 units = 2 340, 1 unit = 468). 2) (3 + 5) × 6 − 2 = 8 × 6 − 2 = 46. 3) 12 ÷ 4 × 5 = 15 (the only way). 4) Multiplying by 5 and then dividing by 5 gets back to your number. The 35 divided by 5 adds 7. Taking away your number leaves the 7. So the answer is always 7.

p4l3-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q6. Answers: 1) 2 ways: 1 − 2 + 3 + 4 − 5 + 6 = 7 and 1 + 2 − 3 − 4 + 5 + 6 = 7. 2) $48 (work backwards: 9 × 2 = 18, 18 + 6 = 24, 24 × 2 = 48).

p4l3-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: In Q1, what is the total if every sign is +? If you change one + to a −, how much smaller does the total get? In Q2, where does the bar END? Which part do you know? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l3-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: children usually find one way by guess and check. The "take it away twice" idea proves there are exactly 2 ways: the 1 cannot be changed (there is no sign in front of it) and 7 cannot be made from 2 to 6 in any other way (6 + 1 needs the 1; 7 alone is not a card). Q2: the same working backwards as the machine on page 2: undo each step in reverse order.

p4l3-talk.note: Minutes 80.5 to 85. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: Mei is right. With only + and − we work from left to right: 20 − 8 = 12, then 12 + 2 = 14. Ben worked out 8 + 2 first; to do that we would need brackets: 20 − (8 + 2) = 10. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "How did you know which sign to try first in the missing-sign puzzles?" (estimate: a big target needs ×, a small one may need ÷ or −). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l3-exit.note: Minutes 85 to 87.5. Answer: 8. Brackets first: 3 + 4 = 7; then 6 × 7 = 42; then 50 − 42 = 8. Common wrong answers: 308 (50 − 6 = 44, 44 × 7) and 47 (working left to right inside out). Extension: use four 4s and any signs and brackets to make every number from 0 to 9.

p4l3-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 87.5 to 90. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals.
